In [[mathematics]], a '''Bertrand series''' is a [[Series (mathematics)|series]] of [[real number|real numbers]] of the form
:<math>\sum_n  \frac{1}{n^\alpha (\ln n)^\beta}</math>
where <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> are two real numbers.<ref name="Knopp1990">{{cite book |last=Knopp |first=Konrad |translator-last=Young |translator-first=R. C. H. |year=1990 |orig-year=1954 |title=Theory and Application of Infinite Series |publisher=Dover Publications |isbn=978-0-486-66165-0}}</ref><ref name="Radulescu2009">{{cite book |last1=Rădulescu |first1=Teodora-Liliana |last2=Rădulescu |first2=Vicențiu |last3=Andreescu |first3=Titu |year=2009 |title=Problems in Real Analysis: Advanced Calculus on the Real Axis |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0-387-77378-0 |pages=76}}</ref> They are named after [[Joseph Bertrand]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bertrand |first=J. |year=1842 |title=Règles sur la convergence des séries |journal=[[Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées]] |volume=7 |pages=35–54 |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k163860/f43 |language=fr}}</ref>

For <math>\beta=0</math>, this series reduces to the series <math>\textstyle \sum_n \frac{1}{n^\alpha}</math> defining the [[Riemann zeta function]].

One can show a [[If and only if|necessary and sufficient]] condition of [[Convergent series|convergence]] for such series: it converges if and only if <math>\alpha>1</math> or (<math>\alpha=1</math> and <math>\beta>1</math>).<ref name="Knopp1990" /><ref name="Radulescu2009" /> It can be proved by using the [[integral test for convergence]] or the [[Cauchy condensation test]].

One has the following approximate values:
* <math>\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac1{n(\ln n)^2}\approx 2.10974</math> {{OEIS|A115563}};
* <math>\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac1{n(\ln n)^3}\approx 2.06589</math> {{OEIS|A145419}};
* <math>\sum_{n\geq 2}\frac1{n^2\ln n}\approx 0.60552</math> {{OEIS|A168218}}.
